Ayurveda is practiced for centuries and proved to be helpful in curing various types of diseases.
Over the time, with advancement and modernization of other forms of medicine and continued traditional practice of Ayurveda, the approach to Ayurvedic treatment has reduced.
By establishing the Ayurvedic procedure as per modern scientific methods, its benefits can be made available to the society as an alternate form of medicine.

The well-known Kirchhoff theory is taken into account for the thin plate on elastic foundation.
Analytical methods are developed to analyse the plate on elastic foundation for simply supported (SS) plate in early 1960s' (Timoshenko and Krieger, 1959).
Recently in 2014, the plate on elastic foundation analysis was extended to fixed fixed (FF) plate using double finite sine integral transform method (Bidgoli et al., 2014).
Winkler's model is found to be suitable for plate resting on the continuously distributed elastic springs which act as the elastic foundation (Wang et al., 2005).

The cross-section of the forehead is idealized as an isotropic homogenous elastic plate over an elastic foundation and is given by the governing differential equation for deflection for both boundary condition (SS and FF) (Timoshenko and Kreiger, 1959;Bidgoli et al., 2014).
The anatomy of the forehead includes skin from the surface to the underlying rigid bone of the skull.
The soft tissue includes skin, subcutaneous layer and muscle (Xu and Yang, 2015).
The subcutaneous layer which is a fatty tissue is neglected in the analysis.
The bone which is a hard tissue and rigid is independent of deflection.
Hence, the model of forehead includes skin and muscle; and the human skin acts as a piezoelectric sensor (Shamos and Lavine, 1967).

Skin which is stretchable and elastomeric and sensitive to mechanical forces is idealised as the plate on an elastic foundation of muscular tissues, as the expression for the plate on an elastic foundation is easily available ignoring stretching energy.
There is no existing literature of standard procedure of an attempt to characterise the mechanical and electrical properties of skin and muscle.
Human skin has a permanent electric dipole moment and voltage responses are predicted due to the pressure applied to the skin which is piezoelectric in nature.
These voltage responses are measured as piezoelectric constants in human.
Hence human skin acts as a piezoelectric sensor (Athenstaedt et al., 1982;Rossi et al., 1986;Shamos and Lavine, 1967;Cromwell et al., 1980).
